questions.prompt: What physical component makes a superconducting circuit usable as a qubit rather than just a harmonic LC oscillator?
options: A Josephson junction, which adds the anharmonicity needed to isolate a clean two-level system
A resistor placed in series with the circuit
A capacitor used alone, with no other components
A diode that rectifies the microwave drive signal
questions.explain: A plain LC oscillator has evenly spaced energy levels, so a microwave pulse can't selectively address just the 0-to-1 transition. The Josephson junction's nonlinear inductance creates anharmonicity -- unequal spacing between energy levels -- which is what lets you isolate and address a clean two-level qubit.

questions.prompt: An engineer wants to further reduce a transmon qubit's sensitivity to charge noise by increasing its shunting capacitance even more. What is the most likely consequence for the qubit's usability as a two-level system?
options: Its anharmonicity shrinks further, making it harder to cleanly isolate the 0-to-1 transition from higher levels
Its anharmonicity increases, making gates easier to apply
There is no tradeoff -- charge noise and anharmonicity are unrelated
The qubit becomes completely immune to all forms of noise
questions.explain: The transmon design trades charge-noise sensitivity for reduced anharmonicity: a larger shunting capacitor suppresses charge-noise sensitivity but also further flattens the energy-level spacing. Push it too far and the qubit becomes harder to address cleanly and more prone to leakage into higher states -- a real engineering tradeoff, not a free improvement.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about superconducting qubit coherence times T1 and T2 are accurate, per the relationship 1/T2 = 1/(2*T1) + 1/T-phi?
options: T2 can never exceed 2 times T1
T1 measures energy relaxation (amplitude damping), the decay from |1> to |0>
T2 always equals exactly 2 times T1 for every real qubit
Pure dephasing (T-phi) contributes to T2 in addition to T1-driven decay
questions.explain: The formula 1/T2 = 1/(2*T1) + 1/T-phi sets a hard ceiling of T2 <= 2*T1, reached only in the idealized limit where pure dephasing is negligible (T-phi approaches infinity). In real devices T-phi is finite and contributes its own term, so T2 is almost always strictly less than 2*T1 -- it is not 'always exactly' 2*T1.

questions.prompt: A dilution refrigerator cools a superconducting quantum chip to roughly what temperature scale -- name the unit (thousandths of a degree above absolute zero)?
questions.explain: Superconducting qubits are cooled to roughly 10-20 millikelvin, deep in the millikelvin regime, both to maintain superconductivity and to suppress thermal microwave photons that would otherwise randomly disturb the qubit's state.

questions.prompt: A news article claims: 'Company A's new superconducting chip has more qubits than Company B's, so it is strictly the more capable quantum computer.' Which single additional piece of information would most directly challenge this conclusion?
options: Company A's stock price relative to Company B's
The physical dimensions of each company's cryostat
Company A's two-qubit gate fidelity and its chip's connectivity graph
Which company announced its chip first
questions.explain: Raw qubit count alone doesn't determine what a device can actually run -- fidelity and connectivity matter just as much. A chip with more qubits but worse gate fidelity or a sparser connectivity graph can be less useful in practice than a smaller, more reliable, better-connected one.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are real, honestly stated tradeoffs of trapped-ion qubits relative to superconducting qubits, per this course?
options: Trapped-ion two-qubit gates are typically slower (microseconds) than superconducting gates (nanoseconds)
Ion chains offer all-to-all connectivity within a single chain, unlike fixed-neighbor superconducting wiring
Trapped-ion qubits require a dilution refrigerator at millikelvin temperatures, exactly like superconducting qubits
Motional mode crowding limits how long a single ion chain can practically scale
questions.explain: Trapped ions are held in room-temperature-compatible vacuum traps using lasers and RF fields, not a dilution refrigerator -- that's a superconducting-qubit requirement, not a trapped-ion one. The real trapped-ion tradeoffs are slower gates and chain-length scaling limits from motional mode crowding, offset by the real advantage of all-to-all connectivity within a chain.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the standard trapped-ion two-qubit gate that entangles two ions by coupling each to a shared motional (phonon) mode via detuned laser pulses?
questions.explain: The Mølmer–Sørensen (MS) gate is the standard trapped-ion two-qubit gate. It entangles two ions indirectly, by coupling each one's internal qubit state to the ion chain's shared vibrational (motional/phonon) mode, which acts as the communication channel between ions.

questions.prompt: A trapped-ion vendor advertises 'full all-to-all connectivity' for its processor. Based on motional mode crowding, what is the most accurate qualification to add to that claim?
options: The claim is true without any qualification and holds at any chain length
This holds within a single ion chain, but longer chains face increasingly crowded, closely spaced motional modes that limit practical chain length and scaling
All-to-all connectivity is purely a marketing term with no physical basis whatsoever
All-to-all connectivity only works if the system is cooled below absolute zero
questions.explain: All-to-all connectivity within one ion chain is real and is trapped-ion's headline architectural advantage. But it isn't unlimited: as a chain gets longer, its motional modes become more closely spaced and harder to address cleanly, which is exactly why vendors pursue ion shuttling and multi-zone (QCCD) architectures to scale beyond a single chain's practical length.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly describe the QCCD (quantum charge-coupled device) architecture used by companies like Quantinuum?
options: It divides a trap into multiple zones and physically shuttles ions between them
It is used specifically to scale beyond what a single ion chain's motional modes can practically support
It eliminates the need for laser-based gates entirely
It is a purely superconducting-chip fabrication technique
questions.explain: QCCD architectures shuttle ions between physically separate trap zones so gates can happen within smaller, manageable sub-chains rather than one ever-longer chain -- directly addressing motional-mode crowding. It's a trapped-ion-specific technique, not a superconducting one, and it still relies on laser-driven gates within each zone.

questions.prompt: A friend claims trapped-ion computers are 'strictly better' than superconducting computers because reported two-qubit gate fidelities are often higher. Which response best explains why this conclusion doesn't follow?
options: All reported fidelity numbers are fabricated and should be ignored
Fidelity is only one dimension -- gate speed and chain-length/motional-mode scaling limits are real countervailing tradeoffs that fidelity alone doesn't capture
Trapped-ion systems have no real advantages at all
Superconducting qubits always have higher fidelity in practice, so the premise is simply false
questions.explain: The course frames this explicitly as an engineering tradeoff, not a strict ranking: higher reported two-qubit fidelity on trapped-ion systems comes alongside slower gate times and chain-length scaling limits, while superconducting systems trade some fidelity for speed and a different (wiring-density) scaling bottleneck. No single dimension settles which platform is 'better' overall.

questions.prompt: What is the dominant, largely uncorrectable source of error in photonic quantum computing, since a lost photon simply cannot be recovered?
questions.explain: Unlike a superconducting or ion qubit that degrades gradually via decoherence, a photon that is absorbed, scattered, or missed by a detector is simply gone -- there's no 'storing' it to try again. This makes photon loss the dominant and largely uncorrectable error source in photonic quantum computing.

questions.prompt: Which statements accurately describe photonic quantum computing's real advantages and limitations, per this course?
options: It can operate at room temperature, unlike superconducting qubits, which need a dilution refrigerator
Photon loss is largely uncorrectable because a lost photon cannot simply be recovered
It is currently ahead of superconducting and trapped-ion platforms for universal fault-tolerant computing
Some linear-optical two-qubit gates are inherently probabilistic and require heralding to confirm success
questions.explain: Photonic QC's real advantages are room-temperature operation and natural networking; its real cost is that some gates are probabilistic (needing heralding) and photon loss is hard to correct. The course is explicit that photonic approaches are generally earlier-stage for universal fault tolerance than superconducting or trapped-ion platforms, not ahead of them.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the strong, distance-dependent interaction between neutral atoms excited to high-energy states, used to implement entangling gates in neutral-atom quantum computers?
questions.explain: When a neutral atom is excited to a Rydberg state, it becomes effectively much larger and strongly interacts with nearby Rydberg atoms. This Rydberg blockade effect creates a strong, controllable interaction that neutral-atom platforms use to implement entangling gates between atoms held in optical tweezers.

questions.prompt: A news article claims a neutral-atom company's processor 'now has the most qubits of any quantum computer in the world.' What question should you ask before treating this as evidence the system is close to outperforming other platforms on real computations?
options: None -- raw qubit count alone settles the comparison
What are the actual two-qubit gate fidelities and atom-loss/reload rates, and how many of those atoms are usable as reliable logical qubits versus just raw trapped atoms?
What color are the trapping lasers?
How many investors has the company raised funding from?
questions.explain: The course is explicit that large raw atom counts are genuinely achievable because loading/trapping neutral atoms scales well, but that doesn't equal usable computational power -- gate fidelity, atom loss and reloading, and connectivity during rearrangement are the real open challenges, and raw qubit count is not the same as error-corrected, usable logical qubits.

questions.prompt: When comparing superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic, and neutral-atom modalities, which platform-to-primary-scaling-bottleneck pairings are accurate per this course?
options: Superconducting -- cryostat wiring density and heat load
Trapped-ion -- motional mode crowding in long chains
Photonic -- photon loss
Neutral-atom -- has no real scaling bottleneck at all
questions.explain: Every modality taught in this course has a real, honestly stated scaling bottleneck -- superconducting (wiring/heat load), trapped-ion (motional mode crowding), photonic (photon loss), and neutral-atom (atom loss, 2D-rearrangement connectivity, and gate fidelity gaps, despite impressive raw atom counts). None is bottleneck-free.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the superconducting qubit chip layout IBM uses, based on a hexagonal pattern chosen to reduce frequency collisions at the cost of some connectivity?
questions.explain: IBM's heavy-hex lattice connects each qubit to fewer neighbors than a dense square grid would, but this sparser layout reduces the chance that two physically close qubits have resonant frequencies similar enough to interfere (a frequency collision) -- a deliberate connectivity-for-reliability tradeoff.

questions.prompt: A two-qubit gate needs to be applied between two physical qubits that are graph-distance 3 apart on a device's connectivity graph. Each SWAP moves a qubit's state one edge closer and is typically built from 3 CNOTs on superconducting hardware. Roughly how many extra two-qubit gates (beyond the 1 target gate itself) does routing this single interaction require?
options: 1 extra gate
3 extra gates
6 extra gates
9 extra gates
questions.explain: Closing a graph-distance of 3 down to adjacency (distance 1) requires 2 SWAPs. At 3 CNOTs per SWAP, that's 2 x 3 = 6 extra two-qubit gates, on top of the 1 target gate -- 7 total two-qubit operations for what was logically a single gate.

questions.prompt: Which statements accurately describe SWAP gates and routing overhead, per this course?
options: A SWAP gate exchanges the quantum states held by two qubits
On superconducting hardware, a SWAP is typically built from 3 CNOT gates in sequence
Routing overhead can never become the dominant source of error in a circuit
Compilers use heuristic routing algorithms because finding the provably optimal SWAP network is computationally expensive for most circuits
questions.explain: The course works through a concrete example where SWAP-derived gates push a circuit's total error from roughly 18% to roughly 39% -- more than half of the total error coming purely from routing. So routing overhead absolutely can become the dominant error source on circuits with poor connectivity matches, contrary to option C.

questions.prompt: You're choosing between two qubit regions on the same chip for your circuit: Region A offers your circuit's needed connectivity natively (no SWAPs) but middling two-qubit error rates; Region B has excellent error rates but requires inserting 2 extra SWAPs. What would you need to quantify before deciding between them?
options: Whether the combined error from Region B's 2 extra SWAPs (6 extra gates) exceeds the error Region A incurs from its native but higher per-gate error rate
Which region looks better on the provider's marketing page
Nothing -- always pick whichever region has the best raw error rate, regardless of SWAP count
Nothing -- always avoid any region requiring SWAPs, regardless of its error rate
questions.explain: Neither 'best error rate' nor 'fewest SWAPs' alone is the right rule -- the real decision requires comparing total accumulated error: Region A's native-but-higher per-gate error versus Region B's lower per-gate error multiplied across more total gates (the original circuit plus 6 extra SWAP-derived gates).

questions.prompt: Which of the following are genuinely part of the classical control stack supporting a 'quantum' computer, per this course?
options: Arbitrary waveform generators (AWGs) operating at room temperature
HEMT and parametric amplifiers in the readout chain
The qubits' own intrinsic measurement, requiring no external electronics at all
FPGAs used for real-time feedback and control
questions.explain: Every real 'quantum' computer is actually a hybrid classical-quantum system: room-temperature AWGs and FPGAs generate and process control signals, and cryogenic HEMT/parametric amplifiers boost faint readout signals on the way back out. Qubits cannot be driven or measured without this surrounding classical electronics stack.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the shaped-pulse technique used in superconducting qubit control to suppress unwanted leakage to higher energy levels outside the intended two-level subspace?
questions.explain: A DRAG (Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate) pulse shapes a control pulse's amplitude and phase specifically to cancel out unwanted population leaking into the qubit's higher, non-computational energy levels, improving gate fidelity or speed beyond a naive default pulse shape.

questions.prompt: A team submits a long, sensitive circuit to a real device at 2 PM, relying on a calibration report generated at 6 AM that morning. What is the most accurate concern here, per this course's treatment of calibration drift?
options: None -- once a device is calibrated, its parameters never change again

Qubit frequencies, coherence times, and error rates can drift over the intervening hours due to thermal fluctuations, material defects, or flux noise, so the 6 AM report may no longer reflect the device's current state
The circuit will automatically recalibrate itself the moment it is submitted
Calibration drift is a concern only for photonic quantum computers, not superconducting ones
questions.explain: The course is explicit that a published calibration report is a snapshot, not a permanent guarantee -- qubit parameters genuinely drift over minutes to days, which is why providers run periodic recalibration jobs and why practitioners should be cautious trusting calibration data that may be many hours stale.

questions.prompt: Which fields would you realistically expect to find in a real backend calibration report, per this course?
options: Per-qubit T1 and T2
Per-edge (per-qubit-pair) two-qubit gate error rate
The physical color of the chip's packaging
A last-calibrated timestamp
questions.explain: A real calibration report is built from measured, operationally relevant data -- per-qubit coherence times, per-edge gate error rates, readout error, and a timestamp showing how recently that data was measured -- not cosmetic details about the hardware's physical appearance.

questions.prompt: A vendor announces a new 500-qubit chip and says nothing about its two-qubit gate fidelity or its connectivity graph. Per the 'three-way AND' rule from this course, what should you conclude?
options: The chip is automatically the most capable quantum computer available
You cannot yet judge what real circuits this chip can actually run, because qubit count alone doesn't guarantee sufficient fidelity or connectivity
500 qubits guarantees a high Quantum Volume score
The announcement must be fraudulent
questions.explain: The course's 'three-way AND' framework holds that qubit count, coherent circuit depth (driven by fidelity), and connectivity must all be sufficient together -- a high qubit count with unstated or poor fidelity and connectivity tells you very little about what the device can actually, reliably compute.

questions.prompt: Device A reports a Quantum Volume of 128, and Device B reports a Quantum Volume of 64. Using QV = 2^n, what does this comparison tell you about the largest 'square' circuit size (n) each device can reliably run?
options: Device A reliably reaches n=7 (a 7-qubit, 7-layer circuit), while Device B reaches n=6 (6-qubit, 6-layer) -- a real, nontrivial jump in capability, not a huge one
Device A simply has exactly twice as many physical qubits as Device B
Device A can run any circuit of any depth, as long as it uses 128 or fewer qubits
The comparison tells you nothing meaningful about either device
questions.explain: Since QV = 2^n, a QV of 128 means n=7 and a QV of 64 means n=6 (2^7=128, 2^6=64). This reflects the largest random square circuit each device reliably passes, not raw qubit count -- QV folds qubit count, fidelity, and connectivity into the single n value, and doubling QV from one step of n to the next represents a real but incremental capability jump, not a doubling of qubit count.

questions.prompt: Which statements accurately describe IBM's Quantum Volume (QV) benchmark, per this course?
options: QV folds qubit count, connectivity, and gate fidelity (via its pass/fail threshold on random square circuits) into a single number
A device can score well on QV purely by having a very large raw qubit count, regardless of fidelity or connectivity
QV uses one specific statistical family of random circuits, so it may not reflect how a device handles a particular structured algorithm
CLOPS measures execution speed, a dimension that QV itself does not capture
questions.explain: QV circuits grow in both width and depth together, so a device cannot pass a high-n test just by having many qubits -- it also needs the fidelity and connectivity to survive that many layers. QV is also just one circuit family, which is why other composite metrics like CLOPS (speed) and algorithmic qubits exist to capture dimensions QV leaves out.

questions.prompt: A research team needs a 12-qubit chemistry simulation with a deep circuit, where several non-adjacent qubit pairs must interact directly. Which factor would most favor a trapped-ion platform over a superconducting one for this specific workload?
options: Trapped-ion's all-to-all connectivity within a chain reduces the need for SWAP-based routing for those non-adjacent interactions
Trapped-ion gates are always faster than superconducting gates
Trapped-ion systems never experience any decoherence
Superconducting chips are physically incapable of running any 12-qubit circuit
questions.explain: The deciding factor here is connectivity, not speed or an exaggerated decoherence claim: a workload needing many non-adjacent qubit pairs to interact directly plays to trapped-ion's real headline advantage (all-to-all connectivity within a chain), avoiding the SWAP overhead a fixed-neighbor superconducting layout would require.

questions.prompt: Per this course's capstone framework, which elements belong in a well-constructed hardware-selection brief?
options: A requirements summary describing the actual workload
The candidate platforms considered and the specific deciding tradeoff between them
An honestly stated caveat or risk of the recommended choice
A guarantee that the recommendation will never need to change
questions.explain: The course's five-section brief structure includes requirements, candidates considered, the deciding tradeoff, the recommendation with honest caveats, and a stated revisit condition -- explicitly NOT a false guarantee of permanence. A good brief tells the reader what would change the recommendation, not that it never will.

questions.prompt: What term does this course use for a vendor's tendency to promote whichever composite hardware benchmark happens to favor their own architecture's strengths?
questions.explain: The course names this pattern explicitly: a superconducting vendor emphasizing Quantum Volume, a trapped-ion vendor emphasizing algorithmic qubits, and another vendor emphasizing CLOPS may each be stating true numbers about their own hardware, while each foregrounds the benchmark that flatters their own architecture -- benchmark bias.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a fidelity-adjusted, qubit-count-like metric promoted by some trapped-ion vendors, distinct from IBM's Quantum Volume?
options: CLOPS
Algorithmic qubits
Heavy-hex lattice
DRAG pulse
questions.explain: Algorithmic qubits is a metric, promoted by some trapped-ion vendors, that attempts to express how many 'good enough' qubits a device effectively provides once realistic error rates are accounted for -- distinct from CLOPS (a speed metric) and unrelated to the heavy-hex lattice (a connectivity layout) or DRAG pulses (a pulse-shaping technique).
